channel.title: I Will Not Look Away — International law, applied to everyone
channel.description: Violations of international law, from Gaza to Ukraine to Sudan: analysis, current affairs and manifestos with the rule cited, a dated source and the same standard for all.

item.title: Europe stopped depending on Moscow. Who does it depend on now?
item.description: The EU cut Russian gas faster than expected, but households pay almost twice as much for gas and the new dependence lies across the Atlantic.

item.title: Three years since October 7
item.description: On 7 October 2023 about 1,200 people were killed in Israel and 251 were taken to Gaza as hostages. Three years on, a remembrance.

item.title: Outside the fence
item.description: In 2026 artificial intelligence models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta escaped their test environments and entered real systems. The incidents, the causes, the missing rules.

item.title: How to govern a machine: the tools on the table for regulating artificial intelligence
item.description: Nine tools for regulating artificial intelligence, from incident reporting to a treaty on autonomous weapons: where they exist, who proposes them, what the objections are.

item.title: Six roads for artificial intelligence: the possible scenarios and the signals to watch
item.description: Six scenarios for the future of artificial intelligence, from the unchecked race to promises kept: what facts they grow out of and what signals to watch.

item.title: Minab, the school nobody checked
item.description: On February 28, 2026, a US missile destroyed a school in Minab, Iran. Old data, an artificial intelligence system, cuts to oversight: the chain of errors and who is accountable.

item.title: Who is putting on the brakes?
item.description: The ones calling for a slowdown are the same people running the fastest companies, and those who should apply the brakes reply that a strong president is all it takes. An opinion on artificial intelligence, war and who is accountable.

item.title: Ethiopia, the war no one is covering: a guide to understanding it
item.description: Since 23 September Ethiopia has been at war again: Abiy Ahmed's government against an alliance of seven armed groups, with Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt accused of backing it. Who is fighting, why, and what is at stake from the Red Sea to the Nile and the Horn of Africa.

item.title: Ecuador, war by decree: calling crime a war to change the rules
item.description: Ecuador has the highest homicide rate in Latin America. The government responds by declaring an "internal armed conflict" that the Constitutional Court has rejected five times, opens the door to foreign troops with immunity and provides for pardons for the military. Meanwhile the Prosecutor's Office is investigating 43 possible enforced disappearances.

item.title: Sudan, war by remote: who supplies, who pilots, who should stop it
item.description: More than a thousand civilians killed by drones in five months, by both sides. A UN report reconstructs the network supplying the RSF across the Emirates, Chad, Libya and Puntland, and the Colombian contractors at the controls. By 9 October it will be decided whether the Mission continues.

item.title: Nigeria: who is killed, who tells the story, who should prosecute
item.description: Washington speaks of a persecution of Christians and bombs with Abuja's consent. Who really dies in Nigeria, who counts the dead, who profits from the confusion, and why the International Criminal Court has not investigated since 2020.

item.title: The condemned woman who did not die. Who still uses the death penalty, and which limits of the law they breach
item.description: Tennessee failed to execute Christa Pike: now she is being treated, and the law allows another attempt. Who still uses the death penalty worldwide, by what methods, and which limits of international law they breach.

item.title: Haiti: the UN renews the anti-gang force for six months. But who controls those who shoot?
item.description: The Security Council has renewed the international force against Haiti's gangs until March 2027. The resolution requires abuses to be investigated and publicly reported, but after a year no public report can be found.

item.title: Anatomy of an interview: the American plan, Zelensky and a defeat presented as inevitable
item.description: An interview argues that Kyiv has no choice but to accept Washington's plan. We checked every claim: some are true, others distorted or contradicted by the data. And the demographic bill the interview does not tally.

item.title: Interests first, order second. And no nuclear power is pushing back
item.description: Rubio at the UN: the United States will never put the international order above its own interests. Venezuela, Greenland, Argentina and Hormuz show what that means; China, Russia, India and Pakistan do not really contest it.

item.title: Who pays for the war? Ukraine's debt, Russia's frozen assets and a rule Europe will have to bend
item.description: Kyiv has a budget hole no one had foreseen, and Europe is lending billions that will come back only if Moscow pays for the damage. How much falls on each European, what is documented about corruption, and the rule that protects Russia's frozen assets.

item.title: Anatomy of an alarm: Russian drones, an anonymous source and two stories without proof
item.description: A Spanish newspaper reports a Russian drone attack on Italy, France or Spain. Rome and Paris deny it. An Italian editorial turns it into proof of an allied plot. The same yardstick, applied to both.

item.title: Kallas and Stark Logistics: a moral compass for everyone else
item.description: In 2022 Estonian prime minister Kaja Kallas urged businesses to choose sides. Until summer 2023 the company part-owned by her husband was still shipping goods to Russia.

item.title: BRICS in New Delhi: international law in the text, and who goes unnamed
item.description: The BRICS declaration defends international law, but among the conflicts it covers it names only Israel. Ukraine and the United States never appear.

item.title: Ethiopia: the peace signed in South Africa that no one defended
item.description: Since 23 September 2026 fighting has resumed in northern Ethiopia: the peace agreement signed in Pretoria in 2022 has collapsed. The UN documents violations on both sides.

item.title: The Appeal That Fell Flat: Trump, the ICC, and the Weight of What Goes Unrecognized
item.description: Trump asks every ICC member state to withdraw and prepares sanctions against the Court itself. Only one country follows. Two days later, Netanyahu addresses the UN under an arrest warrant.

item.title: News, Yes. Judgment, No.
item.description: An independent analysis measures the gap between the facts reported on Gaza and the judgment never rendered. Then the names: Kushner, Adelson, von der Leyen, Germany — the mechanism that makes negotiable what postwar law was meant to make impossible.

item.title: Yemen: war intensifies again and fuels child recruitment, as the UN warns of famine risk
item.description: Over 100 killed since last week between Taiz and Hodeidah, 62 new child-recruitment cases documented in the second quarter of 2026 alone, 6 million people on the edge of famine.

item.title: The UN says it isn’t safe to return to Afghanistan. Pakistan keeps sending people back — even now that the two countries have declared war.
item.description: Pakistan sent 146,000 Afghans back in 2026 despite UNHCR advice against return — while the two countries are now in open war. The stories of those deported, and the same logic already seen in Europe.

item.title: Niger leaves the International Criminal Court while the United States and Italy continue military cooperation
item.description: A drone kills 17 civilians at a Niger market: a possible war crime. Niger leaves the ICC while the US and Italy continue military cooperation.

item.title: Taiwan: the price of a balance no one wants to break
item.description: Since 2022 the “Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis” has been underway: Beijing is shifting pressure from air incursions to permanent naval patrols, while Washington treats the arms it promised Taipei as a bargaining chip with Beijing.

item.title: Minerals for security: Congo's peace has a price, and Congo doesn't set it
item.description: A deal that trades critical minerals for military assistance, a constitutional challenge still pending in Kinshasa, and a UN report on weapons reaching those fighting the same war: the DRC's sovereignty over its own resources passes through several hands.

item.title: Hybrid war, hidden evidence: escalation on two tracks
item.description: Editorial by N3R1-70: the Leipzig drone, the false-flag hypothesis, who profits from the Europe-Russia escalation — with the same caution about evidence, in both directions.

item.title: The reopened breach in the privacy of communications: a European case, a universal standard
item.description: A voluntary derogation on message privacy returns in the EU until 2028: verified facts, legal opinions and the UN standard that concerns every reader, not only Europeans.

item.title: When the word of the most powerful man in the world is worth nothing
item.description: An Iran announcement denied within hours, 28 tariff reversals tracked by Forbes, and a channel — Truth Social — in which the speaker himself holds a financial stake: what happens when a given word stops being worth anything.

item.title: Credibility That Erodes — When You Criticize a Democracy Without Looking at Your Own
item.description: What happens when the three sources that measure democracy show that Italy itself is flawed, declining, autocratizing: the right to judge others erodes if you don't apply the same standard to yourself.

item.title: Abstention as Diagnosis, Not Prescription
item.description: The abstention argument, taken seriously — and its limit: if abstention is the correct diagnosis of a system captured by external constraints, it cannot also be the cure.

item.title: The identification knot: why deportation often remains only a paper threat
item.description: From Ceuta to the new EU Regulation: identifying and deporting people without documents is often impossible, not just difficult. Facts, readmission deals, statelessness.

item.title: Who Said What: Dissent Redefined as Terrorism
item.description: Three US speeches on July 16, 2026 redefine dissent as terrorism. A sourced quiz compares them with Russia, China and Iran.

item.title: A deal that worked, torn up anyway
item.description: In 2018 Trump withdrew the US from the JCPOA while the IAEA certified Iran was compliant. Seven years later: two wars and the death of Iran's Supreme Leader. How a working deal produced the escalation it was meant to prevent.

item.title: The warning from their own generals: settler violence threatens Israel's security
item.description: Over 550 former Israeli security officials warn Trump: settler impunity threatens Israel itself. The OCHA and Yesh Din data behind the alarm.

item.title: Thirteen years to topple a man the West had already given up on toppling
item.description: From the 2011 uprising to a proxy war, from the silent 2017 abandonment to the sudden collapse of December 2024: how a conflict can reopen not through new aggression, but simply because attention shifted elsewhere.

item.title: Thirty years to a war
item.description: From the 1990 verbal assurances to the 2014 Nuland-Pyatt call, from Putin's 2021 essay to the diplomatic window lost in Istanbul: how an escalation is built, step by step.

item.title: The Full-Face Veil and the State: Imposition, Ban, Non-Intervention
item.description: In 2026 the same garment — the full-face veil — is legally imposed in Afghanistan and legally banned elsewhere: a comparison of four state models, with a symmetry test.

item.title: How Europe could end up at war without choosing it
item.description: A declared foresight exercise, built on real incidents: drone incursions on NATO's eastern flank, British bases hit in Iran, and what diplomacy should do to contain the risk before it's too late.

item.title: The Veil That Covers the Face: A Shared Root, Three Different Paths
item.description: Christian women with headscarves, Orthodox Jewish women with wigs, most Muslim women with the hijab: the same legal origin produces, in one minority current of Islam, the only outcome that also covers the face.

item.title: Fifteen Years for a Warrant
item.description: On 12 December 2025 a Moscow court convicted the ICC's chief prosecutor and eight judges in absentia over the warrant against Putin. Eleven months earlier, Washington had chosen sanctions for the same reason, against a different warrant: Netanyahu. Two powers, two tools, the same conduct.

item.title: Two warrants, zero arrests
item.description: Putin unarrested in Mongolia (2024) and Tajikistan (2025); Netanyahu unarrested in Hungary (2025). Same ICC warrants, the same single consequence: a referral to the Assembly of States Parties with no coercive power.

item.title: The UN says it isn’t safe to return to Syria. Turkey and Germany are sending people back anyway.
item.description: Syria in 2026: UNHCR rules out safe return, calling non-refoulement a peremptory norm, while Turkey and Germany push for repatriations. A symmetry test between two very different states.

item.title: Three States, One Treaty, Three Different Standards
item.description: On July 22, 2026 the United States signed a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia that abandons the 2009 nonproliferation standard, while Iran is under attack over an IAEA safeguards violation and Israel remains outside the NPT without ever facing a sanction in 57 years: three states, one legal regime, three different standards.

item.title: The stomach for war: who decides, and who pays
item.description: An opinion piece prompted by Nathalie Tocci's Economist article: European troops in Ukraine as a post-ceasefire measure, the democratic-mandate gap in the intergovernmental agreement, and the comparison with Ukrainian public opinion consulted on the same guarantees.

item.title: Colombia: a 2016 peace deal, and children recruited at gunpoint in 2025
item.description: In Colombia's Catatumbo region, the ELN forced over 64,000 people to flee; child recruitment rose 81% in a year.

item.title: Ethiopia: the war the government still calls a “security problem”
item.description: In Amhara, since 2023, the Ethiopian army and the Fano militia have fought with the same methods: summary executions, drone strikes on civilians, forced disappearances.

item.title: A Mayor, an Arrest Warrant, and a Question No One Really Wants to Ask
item.description: New York's mayor is weighing whether to enforce the ICC warrant against Netanyahu. The case exposes the Court's structural limit: enforceable only where there is political will.

item.title: A billion dollars despite sanctions: how Iran keeps funding Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis
item.description: US Treasury Under Secretary John Hurley (November 9, 2025) confirms Iran funnelled roughly a billion dollars to Hezbollah in 2025 despite sanctions. Together with Atlantic Council, State Department and Treasury data on Hamas and the Houthis, the picture shows a systematic funding network behind the Axis of Resistance.

item.title: The paradox of flows: when the same hand arms its own enemy
item.description: Six news pieces verified by this site — Qatar-Hamas, Timber Sycamore, the CIA black sites, Russia's Africa Corps in Mali, Turkish and Chinese drones in Libya, Iran's billion dollars to Hezbollah — show the same mechanism at work across six different governments: funding an armed group you don't directly control.

item.title: Turkish and Chinese drones for Haftar: Libya remains a theatre of UN arms embargo violations, now on both sides of the front line
item.description: Satellite imagery analysed by Reuters (April 2, 2026) shows Turkish Bayraktar TB2 and Chinese Feilong-1 drones at Al Khadim, in the territory of General Haftar in eastern Libya — a violation of the UN arms embargo (res. 1970/2011) now documented on both sides of the Libyan conflict.

item.title: Four European Court rulings condemn Poland, Romania, Lithuania, and Macedonia for hosting secret CIA prisons — no one in the United States has ever answered for that torture
item.description: Between 2012 and 2018, the European Court of Human Rights condemned four countries for hosting secret CIA prisons. The woman who ran one of the harshest sites, where waterboarding was practiced, later became CIA Director. No American official has ever answered for that torture.

item.title: Iran: government admits "thousands" dead in protests, then executes the survivors
item.description: The Iranian government admits thousands of deaths in the January 2026 protests, then executes the survivors: 141 executions in June alone, an 88-day internet blackout, and a leaked internal memo revealing the regime's narrative manipulation.

item.title: Mali: army and Russian Africa Corps mercenaries arrange a corpse into a swastika after killing four civilians
item.description: On June 23, 2026, near Timbuktu, a joint patrol of the Malian army and Russia's Africa Corps kills four civilians and arranges one victim's dismembered body into a swastika — while Mali has already withdrawn from the Rome Statute.

item.title: Israel allowed and encouraged Qatari funding of Hamas for years — a month before October 7 it asked for more
item.description: From 2018 to October 7, 2023, Israel approved and encouraged the transfer of hundreds of millions of dollars from Qatar to Hamas, following a strategy Netanyahu himself declared was meant to prevent Palestinian national unity. A month before the attack, Israel asked for more.

item.title: The United States armed the Syrian rebellion for five years, then shut down the program as a gift to Putin
item.description: From 2013 to 2017, the CIA ran a secret program worth over a billion dollars to arm Syrian rebels. The weapons ended up partly in the Islamic State's arsenal. The program was shut down not for these consequences, but as a gesture of détente toward Putin.

item.title: Three ways to erase a woman: law, body, death
item.description: Institutional submission, genital cutting, femicide are not three separate problems: they are three stages of the same mechanism. An in-depth look with the most current data on Afghanistan, female genital mutilation, and femicide worldwide.

item.title: Yemen: 73 UN staff still arbitrarily detained by the Houthis, as Hodeidah bleeds again
item.description: 73 UN staff remain arbitrarily detained by Houthi authorities as of June 2026, one died in custody; on 5 July the fiercest clashes in years killed 16 government soldiers in Hodeidah. Legal analysis under ICCPR art. 9 and the Geneva Conventions.

item.title: It's Not the Strait. It's the Example.
item.description: An editorial by N3R1-70: the 20% toll and naval blockade at Hormuz are not an isolated incident, but public proof of a double standard — and a dangerous pedagogical lesson for the next generation.

item.title: Rearming for what. An opinion that hasn't closed yet
item.description: Editorial by N3R1-70: a path through Venezuela, Iran and Greenland applies to US conduct the same Art. 2(4) used for Russia — with a stated hypothesis about American debt and explicit skepticism about the existential scale of the Russian threat.

item.title: Cameroon: election crackdown lands in a Paris court, as the Anglophone crisis turns ten
item.description: A universal-jurisdiction complaint against Paul Biya, while the Anglophone conflict counts over 6,500 dead in a decade the Security Council has barely discussed.

item.title: DR Congo: the Washington peace deal hasn't stopped the killing of civilians in the east
item.description: A UN fact-finding mission attributes possible war crimes to every party involved — M23, Rwandan forces, the Congolese army and Wazalendo militias — as fighting continues despite the peace agreements.

item.title: Trump wants Greenland back. And NATO is threatening itself.
item.description: At the NATO summit in Ankara, Trump renews the demand for control of Greenland. Danish PM Frederiksen:

item.title: Trump threatens Iran's water and power plants. It wouldn't be the first time — and it would be a war crime.
item.description: The Iran-US truce over the Strait of Hormuz collapses. Trump threatens desalination plants and a naval blockade; Iran had struck Qatari and Saudi ships to enforce a unilateral route.

item.title: Burkina Faso leaves the International Criminal Court while remaining the world's country most affected by terrorism
item.description: Nearly a fifth of all terrorism deaths worldwide. At the same time, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger announce withdrawal from the Rome Statute.

item.title: South Sudan on the edge of famine, while the tribunal promised in 2018 remains a dead letter
item.description: 7.8 million people in severe food insecurity, 73,000 at imminent risk of death from starvation. The Hybrid Court provided for in the 2018 peace agreement has never been established.

item.title: The jungle advances. But we can stop it with our own eyes.
item.description: An appeal, not a news report: two lists of victims, Arab and Jewish, that international law has betrayed in the same way. With the factual corrections needed on Majdal Shams, the June 2026 UN report, and the Abu Safiya case.

item.title: The blindfold: Europe trading cars for weapons
item.description: An editorial by N3R1-70: Europe's car industry crisis is being used to justify converting car plants into weapons plants — without a European peace initiative to match Europe's rearmament.

item.title: A red card, a phone call, a suspended suspension
item.description: On July 6, 2026, FIFA suspends for one year the automatic sanction against US player Folarin Balogun after a call from Trump to Infantino. This is not a violation of international law: it is the open use of an exemption that already existed.

item.description: On 30 June 2026 the German Federal Prosecutor in Karlsruhe filed charges, before the Hanseatic regional court in Hamburg, against the Ukrainian national Se

item.description: Non-use of force as a horizon, not a description of existing law. Five Middle Eastern conflicts show that diplomacy, when applied, works · 2026

item.title: Hunger Is a Political Choice
item.description: 266 million people do not have enough food. The world knows. The world stays silent. · 2026

item.title: For the Freedom of the Seas — The Seizure of the Flotilla
item.description: Legal, ethical and political grounds for the right not to look away · 2026

item.description: Legal, ethical and political foundation of a coherence Europe owes itself · 2026

item.description: Legal, ethical and political grounds for a necessary consistency · 2026

item.description: Legal, ethical and political grounds for an attention that is owed · 2026

item.description: Legal, ethical and political grounds for a principle that admits no exceptions · 2026

item.description: Legal, ethical and political grounds for a necessary rupture · 2026

item.description: On 8 July 2025 Pre-Trial Chamber II of the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants against the Taliban's supreme leader, Haibatullah Akhundzada

item.description: Italy's request for individual sanctions against an Israeli minister represents the concrete application of the mechanism provided for in ARSIWA arts. 40-4
